title: Russell Jacquet's Eldorado band and the death of his wife
summary: Cobb disputes that Illinois protected Russell, describing Russell's successful Houston band, his move to California and his wife's death.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: Well, has always been very was Illinois sort of protective where Russell was concerned, hasn't he been?
Now you say that in what respect?
Well, it always seemed to me that Illinois would always use Russell on record dates and everything whenever he could; it looked as though he tried to look after his brother.
You know, I'm gonna get awful angry with your conversations.

Let me tell you how this thing happened. Russell had a band at the Eldorado Ballroom during the war days that made a lot of money; had the homestead and he fixed it up. And he was making good money. He would go to the bank on Monday morning and put seven or eight hundred dollars in. Russell had some money. Illinois didn't have nothing. He was working as a side man in Cab Calloway's band. Now you listen to my story.
See, I know what I'm saying.

All right. The Eldorado Ballroom right down the street here on Diamond and Elgin. Russell had a band in there. Russell went to school; he's the smartest one. He went to Junior College at night and came and worked after that at the Club to finish his education.

So he moved, after things had tapered down and everything; his wife was pregnant. He moved to California -- he packed his car up and went out down there and they had a place where they had a place where they had to stay upstairs.
The wife came down the steps one day and slipped, pregnant. And there was a choice of saving her or the baby, the doctor said. So he says, "Save my wife." EN & TAPE Side 3

So after he had said, "Save my wife", it didn't happen that way. She died ... but the baby was saved. Well, his sister stepped in then, Mae, and she had taken care of the girl, but he had schooled her and done everything -- but Mae was the mother, who was her aunt.
